purpose: Ticagrelor is used to lower your risk of having a heart attack or stroke if you have coronary artery disease or have already had a heart attack. It helps keep your blood flowing smoothly by preventing dangerous blood clots from forming in your arteries. It is often prescribed alongside low-dose aspirin for the best protection.
how_it_works: Your blood contains tiny cells called platelets that clump together to form clots. Ticagrelor blocks a specific signal on platelets that tells them to stick together, so they are less likely to form harmful clots. This helps keep your blood vessels open and reduces the chance of a blockage that could cause a heart attack or stroke.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is shortness of breath, especially in the first few weeks — this is usually mild and often improves over time. You may also bruise or bleed more easily than usual, and some people notice minor bleeding from cuts taking longer to stop. Headache and feeling dizzy or lightheaded can also occur.
warnings: Because this medicine thins your blood, you are at higher risk of serious bleeding — including bleeding in your stomach, intestines, or brain. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual bruising, blood in your urine or stool, coughing up blood, or very heavy bleeding. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as stopping suddenly can raise your risk of a heart attack. Always tell any doctor or dentist you see that you take this medicine before any procedure or surgery.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 180 mg (two 90 mg tablets) taken once as a loading dose, then 90 mg twice daily (morning and evening). After one year, your doctor may lower your dose to 60 mg twice daily. Take it with or without food, and swallow the tablets whole or crushed with water. Try to take it at the same times each day.
